title: Decorating halls with crepe paper and the Natchez fire law
summary: Buddy did ceiling decorations with crepe paper for $10-15 jobs; after the Natchez fire a law banned overhead paper; Mr. Tessitore asked him to fix the Tea Room ceiling.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: What kind of decorations would you use?
Well, that was crepe paper, with crepe.
Uh-huh. And you'd cover the ceiling?
Any way you wanted, we'd fix it. That's beautiful. Make it in blocks.
Then we'd twist it. That's beautiful.
Well, and then after the fire in Natchez, what did they have, did they have a, did they pass a law?
They passed a law, no more overhead, or crepe paper. How interesting. And before that, you would decorate the whole ceiling?
Would you decorate the walls too? We used to put wires across the ceiling, and we'd fix the paper over the wires, you know? Yeah, like you can wire. And you couldn't see the ceiling. Yeah.
After we put the paper there, it'd be so many different colors. It was beautiful. People used to come from all over, to come to see different places we used to fix. That's nice.
And was it, did you make it look like seams, like the scouts or something?

No, just blocks, but different colors. You see, we had hundreds of people come at the different ceiling, because that was a big ceiling, you see? Mm-hmm. And when Mr. Tessitore bought the place, the ceiling was in a bad condition, you see? So he sent for me, and he told me to come look at it, and I went look at it. He said, buddy, could you fix this up without me to have to put it in? I said, sure. I said, it's going to cost you a little money for paper. It's going to cost plenty of paper. He said, I don't care, I know it's going to cost me less than buying lumber and stuff. Great paper would be with 50 cents a box then. And he bought the paper thing and we fixed it. And Harold, because people used to come, Harold was playing at the Getsby Tee room there. His wife was working there with me then, she was in the floor show. Rose? Rose DeJong. Yeah, I know her. Yeah. We had eleven, I had 32 people working there counting the band under me. That's a bunch of people.
